text:
# Neural and primitive-based representations

Also called: Neural implicit representations, Neural radiance fields, Neural primitives

## Overview
Neural and [primitive-based representations](#11838-primitive-representation.md) define a continuous scene function $F_\Theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ using a neural network or a set of parameterized primitives to map continuous spatial coordinates (and optionally viewing direction or time) to volumetric signals such as density and color [G]. This family solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry and appearance in a compact, differentiable format suitable for volume rendering and novel view synthesis [G]. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like [Dense grids and memory layout](3-dense-grids-and-memory-layout.md) or [Hash Grid Neural Fields](3855-hash-grid-neural-fields.md) is the exclusive reliance on fully connected layers without auxiliary data structures (like hash tables or voxel grids) to store features, relying instead on the network's capacity and [positional encoding](#876-positional-encoding.md) to capture spatial frequencies [G]. A critical shared challenge is **spectral bias**, where standard MLPs with smooth activations (like ReLU) struggle to learn high-frequency details, often necessitating specific architectural choices or activation functions [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family define a scene function $F_\Theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ using a neural network or a set of parameterized primitives [G]. The input is a continuous coordinate vector (typically 3D spatial position $\mathbf{x}$, potentially augmented with viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$ or time $t$), and the output is a signal vector (e.g., density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$) [G]. The network or primitives are trained by minimizing a loss between rendered observations and ground truth images [G].

Geometric information at a point $\mathbf{P}_{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ is described by the output of a neural network $F(\mathbf{P}_{xyz})$ [S1, unofficial]. Unlike voxel-based methods, in implicit representations the memory usage is constant with respect to the spatial resolution, allowing infinite resolution reconstruction [S1, unofficial]. There are three primary ways to represent geometric information:
1.  **Occupancy/Transparency:** The probability that a point is occupied or its transparency is modeled by a neural network [S1, unofficial]. This allows for semi-transparent objects and approximating occupancy probability [S1, unofficial].
2.  **Level-Set:** The surface is defined as the set of points satisfying $F(\mathbf{P}_{xyz}) = 0$, typically defining the distance to the boundary with a sign indicating inside/outside [S1, unofficial].
3.  **Texture Fields:** RGB images are supported by mapping coordinates to color, taking ray direction into account to support view-dependent phenomena like specular reflection [S1, unofficial].

Rendering involves sampling points along a ray. Common sampling strategies include random points, regular points with random perturbations, or [importance sampling](#9521-importance-sampling.md) near boundaries [S1, unofficial]. For level-set methods, the derivative of distance with respect to the intersection point cannot be computed by autodiff and must be computed analytically [S1, unofficial]. Level-set methods cannot render differentiable silhouette images because the distance to the surface is infinite for background pixels, requiring different loss functions for foreground and background pixels [S1, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [VoISDF Volume Rendering and Adaptive Sampling](821-voisdf-volume-rendering-and-adaptive-sampling.md)
VoISDF is a [neural volume rendering](#1576-neural-volume-rendering.md) method that models volume density as a function of a Signed Distance Function ([SDF](#1466-signed-distance-fields-sdf.md)) to improve geometry reconstruction and enable adaptive sampling. Unlike prior methods that extract geometry from an arbitrary level set of a generic density MLP, VoISDF extracts the surface as the zero level-set of the learned SDF, providing a well-defined surface and inductive bias. It avoids the salt-and-pepper artifacts of random sampling and the density mismatch of second-network inverse sampling by using a theoretical error bound for opacity approximation to drive adaptive sampling.

### [Gaussian Head Avatar (GHA)](1478-gaussian-head-avatar-gha.md)
[Gaussian Head Avatar (GHA)](#1478-gaussian-head-avatar-gha.md) is a neural primitive-based representation for dynamic head avatars that predicts 3D Gaussian parameters directly from facial expression and head pose inputs using multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). It distinguishes itself from mesh-constrained Gaussian methods (e.g., [Gaussian Avatars](#1477-gaussian-avatars.md)) by decoupling geometry from a fixed triangular mesh, instead using a deformation module to predict Gaussian positions based on pose.

### [MAtCha](1487-matcha.md)
[MAtCha](#1487-matcha.md) is a method for high-quality avatar generation from sparse views, specifically designed to handle scenarios with minimal view overlap. It employs an atlas-of-charts and depth estimation as input to a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), which deforms the atlas to produce high-quality meshes represented with 2D Gaussians. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [CoR-GS](#1486-cor-gs.md), which uses heuristic-based independent reconstructions to discard inaccurate Gaussians, by its explicit use of an atlas-based deformation pipeline.

### [Explicit Neural Feature Volume](1838-explicit-neural-feature-volume.md)
[Explicit Neural Feature Volume](#1838-explicit-neural-feature-volume.md) stores neural features as a large, directly addressable tensor, avoiding the [compression](#4-compression.md) into an implicit neural network found in hybrid explicit-implicit models. It solves the problem of reconstruction artifacts and excessive training overhead associated with hybrid approaches, particularly in limited-angle tomography where implicit regularization exacerbates blurring in missing wedge directions. It sets itself apart from siblings like [ACORN](8467-hybrid-volume-mesh-representation.md) by prioritizing reconstruction fidelity and training stability over final storage compactness, accepting higher intermediate memory consumption for better PSNR.

### [Joint Learning with Shared MLPs](2086-joint-learning-with-shared-mlps.md)
[Joint Learning with Shared MLPs](#2086-joint-learning-with-shared-mlps.md) is a strategy for simultaneously training multiple volumetric visualization (VolVis) scenes using a single, lightweight neural network to decode scene attributes from compact anchor points. It solves the problem of redundant computation and storage when optimizing many similar scenes independently by exploiting inter-scene correlations through a shared context model. Unlike separate optimization, which trains a distinct model for each scene, this method groups geometrically similar scenes and shares the decoding MLP across all members of a group, significantly reducing training time and model size while maintaining reconstruction quality.

### [Per-Primitive Color Representations](2582-per-primitive-color-representations.md)
[Per-Primitive Color Representations](#2582-per-primitive-color-representations.md) define mathematical functions to encode view-dependent color for individual primitives (such as surfels or splats) during rendering. They solve the problem of efficiently parameterizing anisotropic or specular appearance per primitive without relying on global neural fields, allowing explicit texture atlases to recover high-frequency details lost by hash-grid collisions. What sets them apart from sibling methods like [MLP Neural Fields](3854-mlp-neural-fields.md) is the direct optimization of per-primitive parameters (colors, sites, lobes) within an explicit atlas, rather than learning a continuous field via gradient descent through a network.

### [2D Feature Fusion](2907-2d-feature-fusion.md)
[2D Feature Fusion](#2907-2d-feature-fusion.md) integrates 2D semantic segmentation and high-dimensional foundation features into a 3D sparse [voxel representation](#10852-voxel-based-representation.md) using Voxel Pooling and Volume Fusion. It solves the semantic gap in neural volume rendering by replacing raw coordinate queries with deep convolutional features, enhancing generalization to unseen scenes. Unlike [standard NeRF](#979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) which relies solely on [implicit mapping](#11979-imap.md) from coordinates, this method leverages multi-view ensembles to smooth inconsistent 2D predictions while using detailed 3D geometry to enable higher-resolution rendering of these features.

### [Structure-aware primitive learning](3157-structure-aware-primitive-learning.md)
[Structure-aware primitive learning](#3157-structure-aware-primitive-learning.md) represents volumetric data using a sparse set of parameterized ellipsoids, optimizing for structural similarity rather than just pixel-wise error. It differs from dense voxel-based methods by explicitly modeling anisotropic structures through covariance matrices, and from isotropic [Gaussian splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) by using ellipsoidal primitives that can capture elongated features more efficiently.

### [Splat the Net](3241-splat-the-net.md)
[Splat the Net](#3241-splat-the-net.md) is a neural primitive-based volume rendering method that replaces the Gaussian kernels of [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) with [splattable neural primitives](#3300-neural-primitive-splatting.md). It represents 3D scenes using a set of parameterized primitives, each containing a small Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) for density and [Spherical Harmonics](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) (SH) for color, allowing for higher expressivity per primitive. The method achieves comparable real-time rendering speeds (>100 [FPS](#7182-farthest-point-sampling-fps.md)) to 3DGS while requiring approximately 10 times fewer primitives for the same scene representation. It builds on [Neural and primitive-based representations](10-neural-and-primitive-based-representations.md) by introducing neural density fields into the [splatting](#23-splatting.md) framework [G].

### [Neural Primitive Splatting](3300-neural-primitive-splatting.md)
Neural Primitive Splatting is a volumetric representation that reconciles the expressivity of neural fields with the efficiency of primitive-based splatting. It represents a scene as a mixture of ellipsoid-bounded primitives, where each primitive contains a shallow neural network defining a spatially varying density field. Rendering computes perspectively accurate splatting kernels via exact analytical integration of this density along view rays, avoiding the costly [ray marching](#6739-ray-marching.md) required by standard neural fields. It differs from Gaussian Splatting by representing the volumetric kernel itself as a neural network rather than a Gaussian function, and from light-field approaches by achieving multi-view consistency by construction.

### [K-planes](3317-k-planes.md)
[K-planes](#3317-k-planes.md) is a white-box, interpretable radiance field representation that factorizes a $d$-dimensional scene into $k = \binom{d}{2}$ 2D feature planes, one for every unique pair of dimensions. It solves the scaling and memory limitations of [dense voxel grids](#1719-voxel-grid-indexing.md) and the opacity of black-box MLPs by using explicit planar features combined via element-wise multiplication. Unlike sibling methods that add plane features (e.g., [TriPlane NeRF](6932-triplane-nerf.md) or [TensoRF](6932-triplane-nerf.md)), K-planes multiplies them, enabling spatially localized signals and allowing a [linear decoder](#3352-linear-feature-decoder-with-learned-color-basis.md) to replace the MLP decoder without quality loss.

### [Neural Geometric Level of Detail](3484-neural-geometric-level-of-detail.md)
[Neural Geometric Level of Detail](#3484-neural-geometric-level-of-detail.md) (NGLD) is a neural representation for implicit 3D shapes that uses a [Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO)](#8749-sparse-voxel-octree-svo.md) to store learned feature vectors, enabling adaptive multi-level detail (LOD) and real-time rendering via sparse sphere tracing. It solves the prohibitive cost of rendering large neural Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by decoupling geometric complexity from the neural network size; instead of a single large MLP, it uses small, shallow MLPs (decoders) that decode features aggregated from the SVO. Unlike [NeuS](6060-neus.md) which uses volumetric rendering, or [MLP Neural Fields](3854-mlp-neural-fields.md) which rely on dense sampling, NGLD enables real-time frame rates by querying only necessary LODs during traversal and blending SDF values for continuous LOD transitions.

### [MLP Neural Fields](3854-mlp-neural-fields.md)
[MLP Neural Fields](#3854-mlp-neural-fields.md) define a continuous scene function $F_\Theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to map continuous spatial coordinates (and optionally viewing direction or time) to volumetric signals such as density and color [G]. This family solves the problem of representing complex 3D geometry and appearance in a compact, differentiable format suitable for volume rendering and novel view synthesis [G]. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like [Hash Grid Neural Fields](3855-hash-grid-neural-fields.md) or [Feature Grid as Radiance Field](5508-feature-grid-as-radiance-field.md) is the exclusive reliance on fully connected layers without auxiliary data structures (like hash tables or voxel grids) to store features, relying instead on the network's capacity and positional encoding to capture spatial frequencies [G].

### [Hash Grid Neural Fields](3855-hash-grid-neural-fields.md)
[Hash Grid Neural Fields](#3855-hash-grid-neural-fields.md) define a continuous scene function $F_\Theta: \mathbb{R}^d \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^k$ by mapping spatial coordinates to high-dimensional feature vectors using a cascade of learnable hash tables at different resolutions. They solve the **spectral bias** problem inherent in standard MLPs, which struggle to learn high-frequency details, by allowing the network to capture fine structures without massive parameter counts. Unlike dense voxel grids which scale poorly with resolution, HashGrid uses [spatial hashing](#5002-spatial-hashing.md) to map voxel coordinates to a compact embedding table, reducing computational operations by approximately 70% compared to direct large implicit network queries.

### [VEG](4089-veg.md)
Not given in the sources.

### [Forplane](5177-forplane.md)
[Forplane](#5177-forplane.md) is a method for reconstructing deformable 4D scenes (3D space + time) from monocular or binocular video by factorizing the volume into a static 3D field and a dynamic 3D field, both represented by 2D neural planes. It solves the problem of efficient reconstruction of deformable tissues in surgical scenes, where tool occlusion and complex deformations make standard 3D [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) approaches slow and inaccurate. Unlike sibling methods that treat time as an independent static volume per step or use displacement fields, Forplane uses orthogonal space-time planes to reduce computational complexity from $O(N^4)$ to $O(N^2)$ while maintaining high reconstruction quality.

### [Feature Grid as Radiance Field](5508-feature-grid-as-radiance-field.md)
[Feature Grid as Radiance Field](#5508-feature-grid-as-radiance-field.md) represents a scene using explicit, low-rank tensor-decomposed feature grids for density and appearance, replacing the implicit coordinate-to-color mapping of standard MLP-based NeRFs. It solves the problem of high memory consumption and slow training associated with dense 3D voxel grids by factorizing the feature tensors into lower-dimensional vector and matrix components, reducing space complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. Unlike sibling methods that rely on [hash grids](#936-hash-grids.md) or Gaussian primitives, this approach maintains a regular, structured grid layout (specifically [balanced spherical grids](#3942-balanced-spherical-grid.md) for egocentric scenes) while achieving compactness through tensor factorization.

### [Atlas-Net](6961-atlas-net.md)
[Atlas-Net](#6961-atlas-net.md) represents 3D surfaces as a collection of independent charts (surface patches), each parameterized by a continuous mapping from a 2D domain to 3D space, learned using neural networks. It solves the problem of representing surfaces of arbitrary topology in a continuous and differentiable manner, distinguishing itself from single-chart methods (like FoldingNet) by allowing local refinement through multiple patches. Unlike sibling methods that may use shared weights or explicit consistency constraints, the basic Atlas-Net formulation defines each chart independently, which offers a better fit to complex 3D shapes but risks inconsistencies in overlapping regions.

### [Dynamic MLP Maps](7360-dynamic-mlp-maps.md)
[Dynamic MLP Maps](#7360-dynamic-mlp-maps.md) is a neural representation for volumetric videos that models the radiance field of each frame as a set of shallow Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). The parameters of these MLPs are stored in 2D grids, called MLP maps, and are dynamically predicted by a shared 2D CNN decoder using a per-frame latent code. This approach solves the problem of slow rendering speeds and high storage costs associated with dynamic neural fields by replacing a single large network with many small, spatially localized networks. It differs from spatial [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) methods like [KiloNeRF](#8942-kilonerf.md) by predicting parameters on the fly via a CNN rather than storing them explicitly, and from tri-plane methods by predicting MLP maps instead of feature maps.

### [Neural Voxel Fields](7824-neural-voxel-fields.md)
[Neural Voxel Fields](#7824-neural-voxel-fields.md) replace the single implicit function of standard MLP-based radiance fields with a voxel-bounded implicit representation, where trainable embeddings are assigned to grid vertices and aggregated by a small decoder to predict color and density. This approach decouples spatial indexing from the neural query, enabling faster training than vanilla NeRF while avoiding the memory explosion of dense 3D feature grids.

### [Viewshed Fields (VF) Learning](7849-viewshed-fields-vf-learning.md)
[Viewshed Fields (VF) Learning](#7849-viewshed-fields-vf-learning.md) is a method that learns an implicit probability distribution over oriented points (location $\mathbf{x}$ and viewing direction $\mathbf{d}$) to identify regions of a 3D scene that are likely to be visible from original camera viewpoints. It solves the problem of generating geometrically consistent novel views and initializing NeRF registration by mapping the distribution of valid oriented points to a simple latent Gaussian space using Normalizing Flows (NF). Unlike standard NeRF rendering which traverses rays to estimate density and color, VF Learning explicitly models the likelihood of a view being valid, allowing for direct sampling of high-confidence camera configurations.

### [Hybrid Volume-Mesh Representation](8467-hybrid-volume-mesh-representation.md)
VMesh is a hybrid 3D representation that combines a textured triangular mesh for primary geometry with an auxiliary sparse volume to capture subtle, thin structures that are difficult to represent with polygons alone. It solves the trade-off between the editability and [rendering efficiency](#12180-sorting-and-rendering-pipeline-optimization.md) of meshes and the high-fidelity detail capture of [neural volumes](#912-neural-volumes.md), enabling real-time view synthesis (2K 60FPS) on consumer devices. Unlike methods that use meshes only as geometric guidance for volume rendering, VMesh renders the mesh directly for its surface appearance while using the volume to enhance specific regions, allowing for compact storage (<50MB) and integration into standard graphics pipelines.

### [Primitive-bound feature embedding](9161-primitive-bound-feature-embedding.md)
[Primitive-bound feature embedding](#9161-primitive-bound-feature-embedding.md) anchors latent feature vectors to a local virtual scaffold that encapsulates each scene primitive, rather than relying on globally fixed grids. This approach solves the scalability and editing limitations of global feature representations by ensuring the feature data moves with the primitives, naturally supporting motion, deformation, and deletion. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Hash Grid Neural Fields](3855-hash-grid-neural-fields.md) or [Explicit Neural Feature Volume](1838-explicit-neural-feature-volume.md) by decoupling the feature storage from the world coordinate system, allowing for high-frequency detail representation within the primitive's support without global memory overhead.

### [Masked Wavelet Representation](9620-masked-wavelet-representation.md)
[Masked Wavelet Representation](#9620-masked-wavelet-representation.md) (MWR) is a compact encoding method for grid-based neural fields that utilizes a multi-level discrete [wavelet transform](#2285-wavelet-transform.md) (DWT) combined with a learnable masking strategy to achieve high parameter sparsity. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption in dense grid representations by removing more than 95% of grid parameters without significant visual quality loss. Unlike standard grid methods or those relying on discrete cosine transforms ([DCT](#8014-discrete-cosine-transform-dct.md)), MWR is specifically designed to handle the non-repeating, non-smooth information characteristic of neural field grids, offering superior compression and representation performance.

### [Marching Neurons](9793-marching-neurons.md)
An analytical method that extracts the exact zero-level set of a neural implicit function by exploiting the piecewise-linear structure of ReLU-based networks, traversing decision boundaries directly rather than sampling space.

#### Neural Anchors
Self-contained "baked" primitives used during inference where the dependency between the feature vector $f_i$ and the global hash grid position is severed [S2]. During rendering, operations such as rigid transformation or non-rigid deformation are performed by simply updating the explicit parameters, with no requirement for retraining or complex volumetric warping [S2]. Each anchor stores explicit geometry parameters ($\mu_i, \Sigma_i$) and an implicit appearance code $f_i$ [S2]. Unlike implicit NeRF frameworks that clip objects exiting the training volume, Neural Anchors maintain full rendering integrity by decoupling the sampling domain from static bounds [S2]. They can be bound to external physics engines (e.g., via tetrahedral cages or mesh skinning) to drive dynamic simulations including gravity, collisions, and soft-body deformations [S2].

#### Anisotropic Neural Representation via Spherical Harmonics
A method that replaces the direct prediction of volume density and latent features with the prediction of Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the scene geometry to be view-dependent (anisotropic) while keeping the MLP input isotropic (position only) [S3]. The anisotropy regularization loss $L_{aniso}$ is the mean squared norm of the anisotropic density and latent features over $N$ samples: $L_{aniso} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} (\|\sigma^{aniso}(\mathbf{d}_i, \mathbf{k}_i)\|_2^2 + \|\mathbf{e}^{aniso}(\mathbf{d}_i, \mathbf{W}_i)\|_2^2)$ [S3]. The maximal degree of the spherical harmonic basis $L$ is typically 3 [S3]. The output dimension of the first MLP $F_\theta$ is modified to $(L + 1)^2$ times the original output dimension to accommodate the SH coefficients for density and latent features [S3].

#### Streamable Hybrid Representation
A technique to handle 4D inputs $(p, t)$ in [hybrid representations](#11926-non-baked-models.md) by streaming feature channels along the time dimension using a sliding window, reducing model size and enabling streaming [S4]. For a $T$ frame sequence, array entry $v$ in $V$ has dimension $F + k(T-1)$, where $k$ is newly needed channels per frame [S4]. Temporal interpolation between observed frames $t_s$ and $t_{s+1}$ is enabled by: $v_{p,t} = \frac{t_{s+1}-t}{t_{s+1}-t_s} v_{p,t_{s+1}} + \frac{t-t_s}{t_{s+1}-t_s} v_{p,t_s}$ [S4]. The method applies to any [hybrid representation](#7846-hybrid-representation.md) $V$ containing feature vector entries, referred to as the backbone [S4].

#### SVGS-NeuralNetwork
This representation shows strong representation ability but has significantly more parameters than the bilinear and movable kernel designs [S5].

#### Neural Network 3D Object Representation
A method where a multilayer feed-forward neural network represents a 3D object by mapping 3D coordinates in object space to a binary output indicating membership [S6]. For objects with simple analytical forms (e.g., sphere, cube), specify the network's parameters manually [S6]. For complex shapes, generate training examples consisting of points on the object's surface, points on inclosed surfaces, and points on enclosing surfaces [S6]. Generate training data using a heuristic that uses the surface normal to determine if a point in the vicinity of the surface belongs to the inside or outside of the object [S6]. Train the network on the generated examples using the back propagation technique [S6]. Test the representation method by repeated evaluations of the network for points inside the object space [S6].

#### Neural Graph Mapping
A [dynamic multi-field scene representation](#11959-neural-graph-mapping.md) composed of small, lightweight neural fields anchored to keyframes in a pose graph [S7]. Fields deform with updated poses during loop closure, enabling consistent volumetric mapping without costly reintegration or fixed scene boundaries [S7]. Merges accurate sparse visual tracking with dense neural mapping in an RGB-D SLAM framework [S7].

#### NeuRBF
A hybrid neural field model that enhances representation accuracy and compactness by combining adaptive radial basis functions (RBFs) with grid-based RBF interpolation [S7]. Introduce multi-frequency sinusoidal composition to extend the frequencies encoded by each basis function [S7]. Decode these features by an [MLP for volume rendering](#2414-mlprender-fea.md) with SDF reconstruction capabilities [S7].

## Background
Neural implicit representations have seen growing interest in representing geometric information in a parametrized manner in neural networks [S1, unofficial]. Early works by [Liu et al](#9228-deformable-beta-splatting.md). [41] proposed the first usage of neural implicit representations in differentiable rendering, selecting the 3D point with maximum occupancy probability along a ray [S1, unofficial]. Mildenhall et al. [42] proposed differentiable rendering for neural transparency, computing pixel values using volume rendering by weighing values of all sampled points along a ray, supporting RGB images and view-dependent phenomena [S1, unofficial]. Level-set methods [43-46] represent surfaces as the zero level-set of a function, typically distance to the boundary [S1, unofficial].
